name: Bicalutamide
lead: Bicalutamide (brand name Casodex) is a nonsteroidal androgen-receptor antagonist: it occupies the receptor that testosterone and DHT normally activate, so those hormones have less effect on the tissue. Its US label indicates the 50 mg dose in combination with an LHRH analogue for stage D2 metastatic prostate cancer, and states that 150 mg daily is not approved alone or with other treatments in the US.[1][2]

For appearance, the interest is in androgen-driven skin and hair problems. Dermatologists have prescribed it off-label, usually in women and often with a contraceptive pill, for female pattern hair loss, hirsutism (excess hair) and acne; a 2025 review describes recent interest in female pattern hair loss and off-label use to improve Sinclair grading.[3][17] Chain: blocking androgen action at the follicle, reduced miniaturisation of scalp hair or reduced coarse facial and body hair, a change in visible density or hair distribution.[12][18] A systematic review of injectable therapy for androgenetic alopecia also lists bicalutamide among agents studied in mesotherapy.[4]

Research for hair is limited to reviews and retrospective data; the large trials are in prostate cancer, where bicalutamide is also a common comparator for newer antiandrogens.[8][9][10][11] The label warns of severe and fatal liver injury, and in men taking it alone breast tenderness and gynecomastia are very common.[2][17] Forum discussion is modest: T Nation members have mentioned bicalutamide in androgen-receptor and post-isotretinoin recovery threads.[5][6][7]

paras: Bicalutamide is a nonsteroidal antiandrogen that selectively blocks the androgen receptor. Unlike castration or GnRH analogues, it does not lower androgen levels; in men taking it alone, testosterone and estradiol rise because the brain's feedback is also blocked.[17] The US label describes it as a competitive inhibitor of androgen binding to receptors in target tissue.[2]

It is prescription-only, is on the WHO Essential Medicines List, and has been available as a generic in many countries since patent protection lapsed (March 2009 in the US).[17] Only the R-enantiomer is active.[1]

Bicalutamide 50 mg daily with an LHRH analogue is the US-labelled use for metastatic prostate cancer; in the EU the 150 mg dose is also approved as monotherapy for locally advanced disease [1][2]. It features in prostate-cancer trials against newer antiandrogens such as enzalutamide and rezvilutamide, and in trials of androgen deprivation with radiotherapy [8][9][10][11].

Wikipedia lists further uses: reducing the testosterone flare at the start of GnRH agonist therapy, androgen-related skin and hair conditions in women such as excess hair growth, acne and hair loss (usually with a birth control pill), feminising hormone therapy for transgender women, peripheral precocious puberty in boys, and priapism prevention, with evidence uncertain for hypersexuality.[17] In Japan the prostate cancer dose is 80 mg per day, and 150 mg per day as monotherapy for locally advanced disease is not approved in the US.[17]

A general reference reports off-label use at low doses for female pattern hair loss and hirsutism, with retrospective studies reporting improvement in up to 53 percent of patients, and a 2024 retrospective comparison with spironolactone favouring bicalutamide [1]. The 2025 review describes its anti-androgenic effect on peripheral tissues and its off-label use to improve Sinclair grade in women [3]. Reviews of the hormonal background of hair loss discuss antiandrogen therapies alongside finasteride and spironolactone [12]. It is also used off-label as an antiandrogen in feminising regimens, and for PCOS-related acne and hirsutism [1].

Androgenetic alopecia is driven by DHT acting on genetically sensitive scalp follicles, which shrink over time; in women thinning is diffuse rather than receding.[18] Wikipedia's androgenetic alopecia article names bicalutamide as an antiandrogen option for women, alongside spironolactone.[18] The off-label route is oral, usually at low dose, and dermatology reviews stress informed consent, contraception for women able to become pregnant, and liver monitoring.[2][3][17]

Evidence for hair outcomes is limited to retrospective studies and reviews: a general reference cites retrospective data in female pattern hair loss and notes unapproved use, requiring informed consent and monitoring [1][3]. A 2025 comprehensive review of alopecia drugs examines antiandrogens among treatments for non-scarring alopecia [13]. No randomised trial of bicalutamide for male pattern hair loss was identified; its antiandrogen action in men is the rationale used in discussions, alongside concerns about sexual and breast side effects [1].

For hirsutism, a phase III trial in Italy tested bicalutamide with a combined oral contraceptive in women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), according to Wikipedia's research summary.[17] Comparator treatments for female pattern hair loss include spironolactone, minoxidil and finasteride; finasteride evidence in women is described as low-quality.[12][18]

The label warns of severe hepatic injury and fatal hepatic failure and advises monitoring transaminases before treatment, at regular intervals for the first four months and periodically after; it also warns of hemorrhage with coumarin anticoagulants [2]. More than 10 percent of patients on bicalutamide plus an LHRH analogue reported hot flashes, pain, asthenia and constipation in trials [2]. A general reference reports elevated liver enzymes in up to 10 percent of off-label users [1].

Wikipedia calls breast tenderness and gynecomastia very common, with hot flashes, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, weakness and raised liver enzymes common, and liver toxicity, lung disease and photosensitivity rare; it recommends liver monitoring, notes that it is contraindicated in pregnancy, and reports that in men with early prostate cancer monotherapy has been linked to more deaths from causes other than prostate cancer.[17] The breast effects are linked to rising testosterone and estradiol when it is taken alone, and it may displace warfarin-type drugs from plasma proteins.[17]

Bicalutamide descends from flutamide, first made in 1967 as an antibacterial and later found to be antiandrogenic.[17] ICI researchers (Tucker and colleagues) selected it in the 1980s from more than 2,000 synthesised compounds; it was patented in 1982 and first published in June 1987 under the code ICI-176,334.[17]

It launched in the UK in May 1995 and was FDA-approved in October 1995 at 50 mg daily with a GnRH analogue.[17] A 150 mg monotherapy dose was approved in Europe, Canada and elsewhere in the late 1990s and early 2000s; the FDA reviewed it in 2002 but did not approve it, and several countries later withdrew the locally advanced indication after negative trial findings.[17] Japan uses 80 mg daily.[17] US patent protection ended in March 2009, after which cheap generics took roughly 87 percent of the US nonsteroidal-antiandrogen market in 2007 to 2009.[17] AstraZeneca reported Casodex sales peaking near US$1.3 billion in 2007.[17]

Bicalutamide competitively inhibits androgen binding to cytosol androgen receptors in target tissue, with the R-enantiomer being active [2][1]. Prostate cancer research has examined androgen-receptor mutations under antiandrogen treatment, including a proposed mechanism for bicalutamide withdrawal syndrome [14][15].

Wikipedia describes good absorption not affected by food, an elimination half-life of about a week (5.8 days after a single dose and 7 to 10 days with continued use), liver metabolism through CYP3A4 and UGT1A9, and passage across the blood-brain barrier in humans.[17]

Prostate-cancer researchers have examined why the drug can lose effect: androgen-receptor mutations selected under antiandrogen treatment can turn bicalutamide from an antagonist into an agonist, a proposed basis for the 'withdrawal syndrome' in which stopping the drug lowers PSA.[14][15] Newer antiandrogens such as enzalutamide were developed to retain activity when receptor expression rises and bind the receptor more tightly than bicalutamide.[19]

Bicalutamide is prescription-only. Its labelled indication is prostate cancer; the label states that it is contraindicated in pregnancy and not indicated for females, so hair and hirsutism prescribing is off-label.[2] It is also used in feminising hormone therapy for transgender women and, with uncertain benefit, has been suggested for hypersexuality.[17]

On T Nation, bicalutamide appears mostly in a few threads. One poster recovering from post-isotretinoin symptoms asked whether it could upregulate androgen-receptor expression [5], another mentioned planning to try it before mifepristone [7], and a 2009 poster said it and flutamide are available antiandrogens that carry more oral side effects [16]. No looksmax.org threads on bicalutamide were found.

Large randomised trials exist in prostate cancer: ENZAMET compared enzalutamide plus testosterone suppression with standard antiandrogen therapy, CHART compared rezvilutamide with bicalutamide in high-volume metastatic hormone-sensitive disease, and RADICALS-HD examined the duration of androgen deprivation with postoperative radiotherapy.[8][9][10][11]

For hair loss, no randomised trial was identified; evidence consists of reviews and retrospective data, including reports of improvement in up to 53 percent of patients and a 2024 retrospective comparison with spironolactone that favoured bicalutamide.[1][3] A systematic review of mesotherapy for AGA (30 studies: 7 interventional, 11 observational, 12 descriptive) included bicalutamide among agents studied, reporting mostly mild adverse events across injectable therapies, with paradoxical alopecia, scarring and dermatitis also noted.[4]

Outside hair, a phase II trial tested bicalutamide in androgen-receptor-positive, oestrogen-receptor-negative metastatic breast cancer, and a phase II trial adding abemaciclib in AR-positive triple-negative breast cancer began recruiting in 2024.[20][21]

lore.intro: Bicalutamide is mentioned occasionally on T Nation as an experimental antiandrogen, mainly in recovery and androgen-receptor discussions [5][7][16].

claims.claim: Bicalutamide might upregulate androgen receptors and help recover from post-isotretinoin or post-finasteride problems.
claims.believers: A poster asked whether it could upregulate AR expression and said they found no studies [5].
claims.experts: No published studies were identified supporting this use; the drug is labelled as an androgen-receptor inhibitor [2].

claims.claim: Oral antiandrogens like bicalutamide cause more side effects than topical options.
claims.believers: A 2009 poster said bicalutamide and flutamide carry more side effects orally [16].
claims.experts: The label warns of severe hepatic injury and lists common adverse reactions such as hot flashes [2].

claims.claim: Low-dose bicalutamide treats female pattern hair loss.
claims.experts: Retrospective data report improvement in some women; no randomised trial is cited [1][3].

claims.claim: Bicalutamide is an alternative to spironolactone for women with androgenetic hair loss.
claims.believers: Dermatology-oriented accounts describe prescribing it when other antiandrogens are not tolerated or effective, and a 2024 retrospective comparison favoured it over spironolactone.[1][3]
claims.experts: Reviews of the hormonal background of hair loss discuss antiandrogens alongside finasteride and spironolactone; evidence for bicalutamide is retrospective and no randomised trial is cited.[3][12]

claims.claim: Blocking the androgen receptor in men would stop pattern baldness.
claims.believers: Posters reason that if DHT acting on the receptor causes loss, blocking the receptor system-wide should protect follicles, and note topical or oral antiandrogens as options.[16]
claims.experts: No randomised trial of bicalutamide for male pattern hair loss was identified; men taking it alone have raised testosterone and estradiol, and breast tenderness and gynecomastia are very common effects.[1][17]

claims.claim: Bicalutamide carries liver risk that requires monitoring.
claims.believers: Forum posters mention oral antiandrogens as carrying more side effects than topical approaches.[16]
claims.experts: The US label warns of severe hepatic injury and fatal hepatic failure and advises transaminase testing before treatment, regularly for four months and periodically afterwards.[2]

card.summary: A prostate-cancer antiandrogen used off-label for women's hair loss; supported by retrospective data only and with a liver-injury warning.
card.note: Label warns of severe liver injury; hair use is off-label.

quick.overview:
Bicalutamide is a prescription antiandrogen for prostate cancer. Dermatologists sometimes prescribe low doses off-label for female pattern hair loss and excess hair.

Evidence comes from reviews and retrospective data rather than randomised trials, and it has little presence in looksmaxxing forums.
quick.mechanism: It binds the androgen receptor and blocks testosterone and DHT from activating it, reducing androgen effects on hair follicles.
quick.risks: The label warns of severe and fatal liver injury and requires liver testing. Hot flashes, fatigue and other effects are common in cancer patients; off-label users report liver enzyme elevation.
